ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Inspection in San Francisco, CA
ut.description: Ultrasonic thickness gauging and UT weld inspection on San Francisco steel frames, bay piers, shipyard steel, bridges and plant piping. Request a quote.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in San Francisco, California
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT performs ultrasonic testing in San Francisco on steel that is hard to open up and expensive to get wrong: welded frames in high-rise buildings, pier and shipyard steel along the bay, bridge members, and process piping that serves the wider Bay Area. The service covers wall-thickness surveys and angle-beam examination of welds, with a written procedure and a report built for engineers and building officials. Tell us the member, material and governing document and we reply within one business day.

Why San Francisco steel gets ultrasonic examination

San Francisco is a dense, seismic, waterfront city, and each of those facts shapes what gets inspected. Dense means tall buildings on tight lots, with steel frames fabricated elsewhere and welded or bolted in the street. Seismic means that the welds that tie beams to columns are designed to deform without fracturing, so a hidden lack of fusion matters more here than in a quiet region. Waterfront means piers, seawalls, ferry terminals and a ship repair yard at Pier 70, where two drydocks, the larger rated to lift tens of thousands of tons, service everything from tugs to cruise ships and naval cargo vessels.

The city also depends on large steel structures that cannot be taken out of service lightly. Bridges across the bay and the Golden Gate, elevated transit structures, the cable and rail systems of Muni and regional rail, and the steel that holds up the airport's facilities all go through periodic examination. The 2013 reopening of the new Bay Bridge east span, and the public attention that followed on fasteners and welds, is a reminder that owners of big steel are expected to keep good records.

Beyond city limits, the Bay Area's refining and chemical complex sits along the Carquinez Strait and the Richmond shoreline. That work is a drive away, but it is part of the same inspection market: piping and vessel thickness programs that serve those plants are planned and mobilized from outside the region.

What ultrasonic testing reveals and where it stops

The probe sends a short pulse of sound into the steel through a couplant. The time for an echo to return from the far surface, combined with the speed of sound in that steel, gives thickness. For welds, a probe set at an angle sends a shear wave through the joint; flat flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks reflect that beam back toward the probe, and the instrument shows the reflection as a peak on its display.

The method has boundaries. It reads what the beam meets, so very rough or flaking surfaces give poor coupling and unreliable readings. Pitting that is narrower than the probe may be missed between readings. Steel with a coarse cast structure, and austenitic stainless welds, scatter sound and call for a modified technique. Steel with laminations can return an echo from the lamination rather than from the far wall. None of these stops a competent examination, but each is stated in the procedure so that the report does not overclaim.

Water on the surface is a San Francisco-specific wrinkle: fog and spray can leave films of moisture and salt on steel, which affect coupling and corrode blocks and cables. Surfaces are wiped dry and re-coupled, and equipment is cleaned and checked after each use.

Wall-thickness gauging for piping, tanks and marine steel

Thickness work follows a simple discipline: define the locations, read them the same way each time, and compare. Technicians use dual-element probes on corroded surfaces, calibrate on a step block of matching material that spans the expected wall range, and read the A-scan so a doubled echo or a lamination does not slip through as a clean number. High-temperature probes and couplants are available for hot lines. ASTM E797 is the contact thickness practice, and ASME Section V Article 23 contains SE-797 for code work; our overview of thickness-measurement requirements shows how the standards connect.

On waterfront steel, the points of interest are splash zones, tidal ranges and under-pier cross-bracing, where wall loss can be uneven and where access may require boats, lifts or rope-free platforms arranged by the owner. At the shipyard, steel renewal estimates on a hull or tank often depend on a grid of readings taken before docking, which lets the owner estimate the steel to be replaced. Note that Atlantis is still in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for ship thickness measurement, so readings taken for a vessel are for the owner's own decisions, not for class credit.

For regulated process equipment, the owner's authorized inspector remains the inspector of record under API 510, 570 and 653, and Atlantis provides the thickness data.

Weld examination in structural and bridge steel

Building steel in San Francisco comes under the city's special inspection regime. The city's form for special inspection puts most structural welding, other than certain single-pass fillet welds and decking items, in the category that calls for continuous visual inspection and nondestructive testing, with a fillet-weld exception. The special inspector is employed by the owner or by the engineer or architect of record, and the inspector's name is given to the Department of Building Inspection's district inspector before work begins. Atlantis can perform ultrasonic examination of groove welds as ordered by the engineer, but the special inspector and the engineer of record keep their own roles.

The governing document for building steel is typically AWS D1.1, with AWS D1.8 for seismic force-resisting systems, and the structural drawings and specification say which weld joints need volumetric examination and what acceptance class applies. Bridge work is under AWS D1.5, and the contract documents set the examination scope. On state bridge work, the contractor's welding quality control plan and the owner's quality assurance program decide who does what; Atlantis works to the procedure and acceptance criteria in the contract and does not replace the contractor's quality control manager.

Technique is the same angle-beam practice used anywhere: 45, 60 or 70 degree probes selected by joint geometry, a reference level built from side-drilled holes, scanning from both sides where access allows, and indications recorded by location and size against the code's criteria.

Records for engineers and building officials

A building official or a structural engineer reading a UT report wants to find a particular connection quickly. Reports for building frames therefore reference gridlines, floor levels and connection marks, and they carry the detail drawing number so the weld in the report is the weld in the model. Where the engineer has specified a sampling rate or a re-test rule after a rejected weld, the report states how that rule was applied, so the next reader does not have to guess.

Photographs of the prepared surface and of the scan layout are attached where they help, because a scan plan on a crowded connection is easier to audit from a picture than from a paragraph. Calibration checks are logged at the start and end of the shift and after any change of probe, cable or instrument settings, and any drift beyond the procedure's tolerance triggers a re-scan of the welds examined since the last good check.

Personnel, procedure and oversight

Technicians work under the company's written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. Level II technicians perform and interpret examinations. An ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports; that role is held in the company by Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies, so qualification records for each technician are held by the employer and available for review.

Atlantis holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates for its management systems. Those do not substitute for a procedure, calibration check or personnel record on a specific job, and the report cites each of those directly.

The company has no office in San Francisco. Technicians are mobilized to the site, and travel and equipment shipping are part of the quotation so scope and logistics are agreed before work starts.

What a San Francisco UT report records

  • Member, weld or line identification with drawing, detail or isometric reference.
  • Procedure number, revision, code and edition, and the acceptance class applied.
  • Instrument, probes, couplant and calibration blocks, with the calibration check at the start and end of the shift.
  • Technician and level, with the Level III who approved the technique.
  • Thickness readings by location, with minimum, average and a sketch of the grid.
  • Weld indications by position, length, amplitude or size, with accept or reject disposition.
  • Areas not examined and the reason, such as access, coating or geometry limits.

Reports are written so a structural engineer, a special inspector or a plant inspector can use them without a phone call to clarify.

Planning ultrasonic work in San Francisco

Urban access sets the schedule. Work on building frames is sequenced with the steel erector, crane and street permits, and examination windows are short because the next trade is waiting. On the waterfront, tides and vessel movements shape access, and shipyard work follows docking dates. Parking, loading and elevator limits matter more here than anywhere else in the Bay Area, so list them in your quote request.

The climate is gentle for UT most of the year. Cool, damp mornings are common, and steel that sat out through a cold night can be colder than the air and collect dew, so surfaces are dried and checked before coupling. Wind on piers and high steel can make instruments hard to handle, and windbreaks or tethering are used. Hills add transport time between sites, and crews allow for it rather than promise tight transfers.

For refinery and chemical plant work across the bay, site orientation and permits at each plant add lead time. Provide your safety and access requirements with the request so that mobilization can be planned around them.

Choosing between UT, MT and PT in San Francisco

Use UT for thickness and for flaws inside welds. Use magnetic particle testing in San Francisco for surface cracks in carbon and low-alloy steel, and liquid penetrant testing in San Francisco for stainless, aluminum and other non-magnetic material. Structural welds often receive UT for the volume and MT for the surface. Our national ultrasonic testing page and the complete UT guide cover the method in general, and the California inspection services page lists related services.

Developing UT skills in your own team

For an owner or fabricator who wants in-house capability, Atlantis offers UT Level 1 and UT Level 2 training under SNT-TC-1A, with practice on the UT simulator. The San Francisco training page explains how courses and employer practical hours fit together, and the eligibility checker shows what experience a candidate needs.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in San Francisco?
faq.a: No. The company has no office in San Francisco, and technicians are mobilized to your building site, pier, yard or plant for the agreed scope, and travel is included in the quotation.

faq.q: What does San Francisco require for structural weld inspection?
faq.a: The Department of Building Inspection requires special inspection, with continuous inspection and nondestructive testing for most structural welding other than certain fillet welds. The owner or engineer of record employs the special inspector.

faq.q: Can Atlantis serve as the special inspector on a building project?
faq.a: No. The special inspector is employed by the owner or the engineer of record under the city rules. Atlantis can perform ultrasonic examination of welds when the engineer orders it and report the results.

faq.q: Can UT be used on bridge steel?
faq.a: Yes. Bridge welds are examined under the contract and AWS D1.5, and ultrasonic examination is a standard tool for groove welds. The contractor quality control plan and the owner assurance program define who performs which examination.

faq.q: Can you measure ship hull thickness at the Pier 70 shipyard?
faq.a: We can take thickness readings for an owner. Atlantis is still in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for thickness measurement, so such readings support owner decisions and are not submitted for class credit.

faq.q: How does fog or salt air affect ultrasonic testing?
faq.a: Moisture and salt film change coupling and corrode blocks and cables. Surfaces are wiped dry and re-coupled, calibration is checked more often, and equipment is cleaned after use near the bay.

faq.q: What is the difference between UT thickness gauging and UT weld inspection?
faq.a: Thickness gauging reads remaining wall with a straight-beam probe. Weld inspection uses an angled shear-wave probe and a reference level to find internal flaws, and the code sets acceptance for each.

faq.q: Does Atlantis replace the API inspector on process equipment?
faq.a: No. On vessels, piping and tanks covered by API inspection codes, the authorized inspector working for the owner carries the responsibility. Atlantis does the ultrasonic work and hands that inspector thickness data and indications to evaluate.

faq.q: How do I ask for a UT quotation in San Francisco?
faq.a: Open the quote link near the top of this page or write through the contact form. Include the member list, material, thickness range, governing document and access limits, and we reply within one business day.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in San Francisco, CA
mt.description: Mag particle testing of San Francisco structural welds, bridge steel, pier and shipyard steel and plant piping. Technicians travel to site. Quote on request.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in San Francisco, California
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT carries out magnetic particle inspection in San Francisco on ferromagnetic steel that has to be proven crack-free: structural welds in building frames, bridge and pier steel, hull and shipyard structure, lifting hardware and pressure-equipment attachments. Technicians travel to your site with yokes, wet and dry particles and lighting, and each indication is reported against the document the project names. Describe the weld, the material and the specification and we reply within one business day.

Where mag particle testing fits in San Francisco work

San Francisco construction is steel construction at a hard scale: towers on small lots, long-span transit and bridge structures, and seismic retrofits of older buildings. Welds in seismic force-resisting frames are designed to yield, and surface cracks at weld toes, access-hole corners and repair locations are the discontinuities most likely to start a fracture. Magnetic particle inspection is the practical check on those surfaces, quick enough to keep pace with erection and sensitive enough to reveal a hairline crack.

On the bay, the work is different. Pier substructure, ferry terminal steel, fender systems and the ship repair yard at Pier 70 involve welded carbon steel in a salt environment. Renewal welds, doubler plates and attachments on hulls and tanks are typical targets, and the method suits steel that is rough, damp or rust-bloomed once it has been cleaned back to metal.

Across the water, the refining and chemical plants of the Carquinez and Richmond shoreline send their steel through outages that call for the same method on vessel nozzles, support lugs and repair welds. Those jobs are mobilized from outside the region, and the planning issues are covered below.

What MT detects and where it is blind

The technician induces a magnetic field in the steel and applies fine iron-based particles. A crack interrupts the field, a small flux leakage forms across it, and the particles pile up on the leakage and outline the crack. The part must be ferromagnetic, which means carbon steel and most low-alloy steel. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys do not qualify, which matters on a waterfront full of both.

MT is a surface method with a little reach below the surface. It finds cracks, laps, seams and some lack of fusion at the toe of a weld, but it does not find deeper internal flaws and it does not size depth. Heavy coatings weaken the field; sharp edges and abrupt changes in section can create non-relevant indications; and magnetic writing from earlier contact with magnets or prior MT can look like a flaw. A careful technician identifies each of these and re-tests where necessary.

Orientation is the other limit. Flux has to run across a crack to show it, which is why the examination is repeated at about ninety degrees to the first pass. Without that second pass a perfectly good test can miss cracks lying parallel to the field.

Equipment and technique on San Francisco sites

Most structural work is done with an electromagnetic yoke. ASME Section V Article 7 requires that an AC yoke lift at least 10 pounds at the maximum pole spacing in use and a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at least 40 pounds, and the technician checks that with a test weight before use. The legs straddle the weld, particles go on as the field is applied, and indications are evaluated while the field is still active. Contrast paint and black particles work on bright steel; dry red or gray powder is chosen when the surface is rough or warm.

Where the highest sensitivity is required, as on critical weld toes or fatigue-sensitive details, fluorescent wet particles are used under UV-A light in a darkened area. In a city of narrow streets and constant daylight, that means an enclosure, a light meter and, often, evening or covered work. Maximum ambient white light and minimum UV-A intensity at the surface are set by the procedure and recorded.

When prods are used on thick castings or heavy plate, the current is set by thickness and prod spacing, and the technician avoids burning the surface with arc strikes. Demagnetization is done if residual magnetism would affect later welding or service, and the residual field is checked with a gauge. If both MT and penetrant testing are needed on the same surface, MT normally goes first, because penetrant residue can block particle movement. Our complete guide to MT goes through technique options in detail.

Codes, building officials and acceptance

The method is controlled by ASME Section V Article 7, and the acceptance rule comes from the construction document. AWS D1.1 governs most building steel and AWS D1.8 adds seismic requirements. AWS D1.5 governs bridge steel. For process equipment, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 provides MT methods and acceptance, and ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.3 with Table 341.3.2 applies to piping. ASTM E709 is the guide and ASTM E1444 the common practice. For a reader-friendly walkthrough, see our explainer on Article 7.

For buildings in San Francisco, the city's special inspection process applies. Structural welding other than certain single-pass fillet welds and deck items falls under continuous inspection with nondestructive testing, and the owner or the engineer or architect of record employs the special inspector. MT performed by Atlantis can be part of the testing the engineer orders, but the roles of special inspector and engineer remain with them.

The State of California regulates pressure vessels and boilers through the Division of Occupational Safety and Health, and its Pressure Vessel Unit has an office in Oakland. Process plants in the Bay Area are also subject to OSHA's process safety management rule, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), which requires inspection and testing to recognized good engineering practice.

Personnel and procedure

Atlantis technicians are qualified under a written practice based on ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician performs the test and evaluates indications, while an ASNT NDT Level III approves the technique and reviews the report. That Level III is Anoop Rayavarapu, qualified at that level in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, so the qualification records behind each report are the employer's and are available on request.

The company is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001. Those are management-system standards, and each MT report stands separately on its procedure, equipment checks and personnel qualification.

The company has no office in San Francisco. Crews are mobilized to the site with equipment and procedure, and travel is part of the quotation.

What a magnetic particle report includes

  • Weld, member or component identification with drawing or detail reference, and base material.
  • Procedure number, revision, governing code and edition, and acceptance class.
  • Technique: yoke, prods or coil, wet or dry, visible or fluorescent, and the particle product and lot.
  • Yoke lift test, light meter readings and any field-strength check.
  • Technician, method and level, and the approving Level III.
  • Indications by location and size with photographs or sketches, and accept or reject disposition.
  • Demagnetization and post-clean steps, where required.

Weld maps for building frames are referenced to gridlines and floor levels so that the owner can find each connection years later.

Evaluating indications and recording them

Once particles gather, the technician decides what the pattern means. A sharp, tight line that holds its shape when lightly disturbed with a puff of air is typically a crack. A fuzzy, broad build-up that disappears on re-test is more often magnetic writing or a particle trap at a rough weld toe. When the call is not clear, the area is cleaned, demagnetized and examined again, sometimes at a different field orientation.

Relevant indications are measured against the acceptance table. Linear indications are compared by length, rounded indications by diameter and spacing, and the code sets the allowable number in a given length of weld. Photographs are taken with a scale in the frame, and each indication is marked on the part with a paint pen so that the repair crew grinds the right place. Repairs and re-examination are tied back to the original report number, so a seismic connection's history remains in one file that the engineer can follow.

If the examination reveals a systematic problem, for example repeated toe cracking from one welder or one procedure, the technician says so in the report and flags it to the engineer, and the decision on how to respond belongs to the engineer and the special inspector.

Practical planning for San Francisco MT jobs

Surface preparation decides speed. Paint and fireproofing must be removed or not yet applied at the weld, so MT is sequenced after welding and before coverings. Coordinate with the erector so scaffolds, lifts and lighting are in place. Street closures, crane picks and permit windows decide when crews can be at the weld; on busy blocks, some work is possible only outside normal hours.

Climate seldom stops MT in this city, but damp steel will hold dry powder poorly, and wet methods need clean, dry surfaces to start. Wind on piers disperses dry powder and tilts tents, so shielding is part of the setup. Cool conditions are a help for wet fluorescent work because carrier fluids stay stable, while a rare hot spell on dark steel needs checking against the procedure.

At shipyards and plants, orientation, permits and escort rules add steps. Send these with your quote request and we will build the plan around them.

MT, PT or UT for a San Francisco project

Choose MT for surface cracks in magnetic steel. Choose liquid penetrant testing in San Francisco for stainless, aluminum or bronze, or when the part is not suited to a field. Choose ultrasonic testing in San Francisco for thickness and internal weld flaws. Building steel commonly gets UT in the weld volume and MT at the surface. See the national magnetic particle testing page, the MT versus PT comparison and the California inspection services page for more.

Qualifying your own MT technicians

Atlantis teaches MT Level 1 and MT Level 2 as theory online, with practical work at the employer's facility under its written practice. The San Francisco training page sets out how that works, and written practice development is available for employers who need to create one.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be done on stainless steel?
faq.a: No. MT needs ferromagnetic material, so austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys cannot be examined this way. Liquid penetrant testing is the surface method for those materials.

faq.q: Why is a yoke lift test performed before MT?
faq.a: It proves the yoke produces enough field. ASME Section V Article 7 asks for at least 10 pounds of lift for an AC yoke and 40 pounds for a DC or permanent-magnet yoke at the maximum pole spacing used.

faq.q: Can MT be used on welds covered with fireproofing?
faq.a: Not through it. Fireproofing and heavy coatings must be absent at the examination area, so MT is scheduled after welding and before the covering goes on. Local removal is possible if the owner allows.

faq.q: When is fluorescent MT needed instead of visible particles?
faq.a: Fluorescent particles give higher sensitivity and are chosen for critical or fatigue-sensitive welds. They need UV-A light and a darkened area, which on a San Francisco site usually means an enclosure or evening work.

faq.q: Does MT find cracks inside a weld?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks and some flaws just below the surface. Internal flaws deeper in the weld need ultrasonic testing, which is why structural welds often receive both methods.

faq.q: Do you perform MT as the special inspector for a San Francisco building permit?
faq.a: No. Under the city process the owner or the engineer of record employs the special inspector. Atlantis can perform MT when the engineer orders it and gives the results to the inspector and engineer.

faq.q: Can MT be done on the waterfront in damp weather?
faq.a: Often yes, once the steel is cleaned to bare metal and dried. Wind shielding is needed for dry powder, and fluorescent work needs an enclosure. Rain or standing moisture normally pauses the examination.

faq.q: Does Atlantis keep a team in San Francisco?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in San Francisco, so technicians are mobilized from outside the city to your project, and the quotation includes their travel and the transport of equipment.

faq.q: How do I get a quote for MT in San Francisco?
faq.a: Use the contact form or the quote link in the first paragraph. List the welds or components, material, surface condition, specification and access limits, and we reply within one business day.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in San Francisco, CA
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing for San Francisco Bay stainless, aluminum and alloy welds, castings and marine parts. Technicians travel to site. Request a PT quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in San Francisco, California
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT performs liquid penetrant testing in San Francisco and around the bay on stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, bronze and other metals that a magnet cannot examine. The work includes weld surfaces, repaired castings, marine fittings and machined parts, and each surface-breaking indication is recorded against the specified acceptance criteria. Technicians travel to the site with materials and procedure. Send the alloy, the item and the acceptance document and we reply within one business day.

Where penetrant testing is called for around San Francisco Bay

The bay is a working marine environment, and much of what floats or services floating equipment is not magnetic. Ferries and fast aluminum vessels, bronze propellers and shafts, stainless deck fittings and heat-exchanger tubesheets come to the shipyard at Pier 70 and to smaller repair facilities. A weld repair on aluminum or a cracked bronze fitting is exactly the case for dye penetrant, since the method works on any clean, non-porous surface regardless of alloy.

On land, stainless steel is everywhere in the regional economy. Food, beverage and wine processing, life-science manufacturing and utility plants all use stainless tanks, skids and piping, and owners or fabricators frequently specify penetrant examination of weld surfaces or of ground-out repairs. Duplex and nickel-alloy components in chemical service around the Carquinez Strait and Richmond are also candidates when a surface crack is the concern.

Architectural and structural stainless adds a smaller category: cable and bridge hardware, stainless anchors and connection plates where a crack from fabrication or fatigue would be unacceptable. Because the technique is indifferent to geometry, a small threaded fitting and a large weld are handled by the same process.

What PT can and cannot reveal

PT can only see a flaw that reaches the surface. Penetrant creeps into a clean crack by capillary action, excess is removed from the surface, and a developer draws the remaining liquid back out so the crack appears as a line or spot. That is all it does. A void inside a weld, however large, stays invisible, and a crack that has been peened shut or smeared by a grinding wheel may not take up penetrant at all.

Several things mask or fake indications. Oil, paint, scale and residue block entry. Wet surfaces dilute the penetrant. Rough ground textures or porous castings hold liquid and glow or stain everywhere. Because depth cannot be inferred, a small surface line may hide a deep crack, so the owner and engineer should decide in advance what follow-up is required if an indication is found: grinding to chase it out, or ultrasonic examination if the weld volume is in question.

The process, step by step

Preparation comes first. The surface is cleaned of grease and dirt, dried and, where blasting or grinding has smeared metal, lightly etched. For stainless and nickel alloys, the penetrant materials are controlled for halogens and sulfur, because residues can harm the metal. Local air-quality rules in the Bay Area district limit volatile solvents, so cleaner and remover choices are made with those rules and the site's own requirements in mind.

The penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left to dwell for the time set by material, expected flaw type and temperature. Excess is removed by the specified method, whether water washable, post-emulsifiable, solvent removable or hydrophilic, as defined in ASTM E165 and E1417. A thin, even coat of developer is applied, and the technician examines the surface after the developer time under good white light or, for fluorescent systems, UV-A in a darkened area. Sensitivity level is selected to match the job.

Temperature control matters in the Bay Area more for cold than for heat. Penetrant systems are normally qualified between 40 and 125 degrees Fahrenheit, and the winter steel of a shaded pier or an unheated shop can fall below that. Dew on cold steel will contaminate a cleaned surface. The remedy is to warm the part, to wait, or to use a procedure qualified at lower temperature.

Choosing the penetrant system and sensitivity

Not every job needs the most sensitive system. Penetrant materials are grouped by type, with fluorescent in one family and visible dye in the other, and by removal method, from water washable to solvent removable. Sensitivity levels run from low to ultra-high, and the procedure matches level to the criticality of the surface and the roughness of the finish. A rough as-welded surface on an aluminum fitting is usually examined with a visible solvent-removable system, because a washable system would leave too much background. A machined stainless seal face or a fatigue-sensitive weld toe is more likely to call for a fluorescent system at a higher sensitivity.

Solvent-removable systems are the common field choice around the bay because they need no water supply and no drain, which suits piers, rooftops and shipyard blocks. Water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems are more often used in shops where rinse stations exist. Whatever the choice, the penetrant, remover and developer come from one manufacturer family and are recorded by lot, since mixing families can change sensitivity in ways the procedure never qualified.

A sensitivity check on a known cracked panel or comparator block at the start of the work shows that the system and the technician are performing as expected, and its result is entered in the report.

Governing codes and acceptance

ASME Section V Article 6 defines the method. Acceptance comes from the construction or repair document: ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8 for pressure vessels, ASME B31.3 paragraph 344.4 and Table 341.3.2 for process piping, AWS D1.6 for stainless structural welding, and the owner's specification for castings and machined parts. See our summary of Article 6 requirements for a plain-language walkthrough.

The code is named by the engineer or owner, never chosen by the inspection contractor. The Atlantis report states the document and edition used.

In the Bay Area, the state Division of Occupational Safety and Health runs boiler and pressure vessel oversight, with a Pressure Vessel Unit office in Oakland. Plants under OSHA process safety management, 29 CFR 1910.119(j), keep inspection records that meet recognized good engineering practice, and penetrant reports often form part of repair packages. For waterfront work, owner and class requirements may also apply, and our maritime scope is limited as described in the FAQ below.

Personnel and oversight

Technicians are qualified under a written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs the test and interprets and evaluates indications; an ASNT NDT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports. Our Level III is the founder, Anoop Rayavarapu, qualified in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT. Employers certify their own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so each report is backed by the employer's qualification record.

The company holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certification for its management systems, and every penetrant job also records materials, lot numbers and procedure revision so it can be audited on its own.

The company has no office in San Francisco. Technicians are mobilized to the site with their own penetrant systems, and the quotation includes travel.

What the penetrant report contains

  • Item or weld identification, alloy and drawing reference.
  • Procedure, revision, code and edition, and acceptance class.
  • Penetrant type and method, sensitivity level, cleaner, remover and developer, each by manufacturer and lot.
  • Surface preparation, part temperature, dwell and developer times.
  • Technician, method and level, and approving Level III.
  • Indications by location, size and type, with photographs or sketches.
  • Disposition against the criteria, and any part of the surface not examined.

Reports for fabricated assemblies are tied to piece marks or weld numbers so that a rejected weld can be found and tracked through repair.

After the indication: evaluation, repair and clean-up

When the developer time ends, the technician reads the surface in order and records each indication before bleed-out spreads. Indications longer than three times their width are treated as linear and judged by length, while rounder ones are judged by diameter and by how many sit within a given area. A cluster of fine dots on a ground stainless surface may be porosity, a texture effect or the start of a crack, and the technician re-cleans and repeats the test rather than guessing.

A rejectable indication is marked, the defect is ground out, and the cleaned area is re-examined. If grinding has smeared metal over the crack, a brief etch precedes the re-test. The repaired area is then tested to the same criteria as the original weld, and the sequence is recorded under one report number for the owner and the engineer.

Finally, residues are removed. For stainless and aluminum equipment that goes into food, beverage, biotech or other clean service, the owner often wants proof that penetrant and developer are gone. The report states the post-clean method used and whether the surface was checked afterward, because a surface that passed inspection but still carries a film is not ready for service.

Planning a PT job in San Francisco

Allow time for cleaning and drying; they are the slowest parts of the job. On the waterfront, tides, spray and morning dew can ruin a cleaned surface, so work is sequenced to keep time between cleaning and examination short. Shipyard work follows docking dates, and pier work follows tide and vessel movements. On city building sites, noise, solvent odor and ventilation rules can limit where and when solvent cleaners are used, and some sites prefer water-washable systems for that reason.

Wind is a recurring factor. It carries dust onto wet developer and can dry penetrant too quickly. Tents or shields help. Cool, damp mornings suit fluorescent work in some respects but demand warm, dry parts. For stainless equipment going into clean service, post-test cleaning and a check for residue are built into the plan.

At shipyards and plants, safety orientation and permits add lead time. Include those requirements in your request.

Penetrant, magnetic particle or ultrasonic testing

Choose PT for non-magnetic alloys and for surface cracks in any non-porous material. On carbon steel, magnetic particle testing in San Francisco is faster and picks up slightly subsurface flaws. For thickness or internal weld flaws, use ultrasonic testing in San Francisco. See the national penetrant testing page, the MT versus PT guide and the California inspection services page.

Building penetrant testing skills in your team

Atlantis teaches PT Level 1 and PT Level 2 through online theory, with practical work done at the employer's facility under its written practice. The penetrant testing simulator lets candidates rehearse each process step. The San Francisco training page explains the arrangement, and practice tests help candidates prepare.

faq.q: What metals can dye penetrant inspection examine?
faq.a: Any non-porous metal with a clean surface, including stainless steel, aluminum, bronze and nickel alloys as well as carbon steel. This makes PT the standard surface method for non-magnetic metals around San Francisco Bay.

faq.q: Can PT detect a crack that does not reach the surface?
faq.a: No. Penetrant testing finds only flaws open to the surface. A buried flaw will not appear, so ultrasonic testing is used when the weld volume needs to be checked as well.

faq.q: Why do cold mornings matter for penetrant testing?
faq.a: Penetrant materials are normally qualified from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Cold, damp steel on a pier or in an unheated shop can fall below that, and dew will contaminate the cleaned surface.

faq.q: What happens if a penetrant indication is found?
faq.a: The technician evaluates it against the acceptance table. A rejectable indication is marked, ground out and re-examined, and the re-test is recorded in the same report series for the owner and inspector.

faq.q: Do penetrant materials damage stainless steel?
faq.a: They can if halogens or sulfur are present. Procedures for stainless and nickel alloys control those contents in the materials, and post-test cleaning removes residues before the equipment enters service.

faq.q: Does Atlantis perform penetrant work on ships for class surveys?
faq.a: We can examine surfaces for the owner. Atlantis is still in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS for thickness measurement, and class-credited survey work should be arranged with a society-approved provider.

faq.q: Is a visible dye or a fluorescent penetrant better?
faq.a: Visible dye suits field work in white light. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive and needs UV-A light in a darkened area, so it suits critical surfaces and enclosed or evening work.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have an office in San Francisco?
faq.a: No. No. The company has no office in San Francisco, so technicians are mobilized to your site with their own materials and procedure, and the quotation includes the cost of getting them there.

faq.q: How do I request a penetrant testing quote in San Francisco?
faq.a: Use the contact form or the quote link in the opening paragraph. Give the alloy, item list, surface condition, acceptance document and access limits, and we reply within one business day.

rt.title: Radiography Alternatives in San Francisco, CA | UT
rt.description: Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US. For San Francisco welds, UT is available where codes allow it, along with ASNT Level III radiograph review.
rt.h1: Radiographic Testing (RT) Alternatives in San Francisco, California
rt.html:
Atlantis does not perform radiography on any San Francisco project, or anywhere else in the United States. Industrial radiography is a licensed activity, governed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's rules in 10 CFR Part 34 or by the equivalent rules of an Agreement State; California is an Agreement State, so the state's radiation control program issues the licences. The company holds no such licence, and exposure work is outside the scope of what it sells here. This page explains what is available when a search for radiography is really a question about weld quality.

Ultrasonic examination in place of radiography

On many San Francisco jobs, the owner wants to know whether a groove weld contains a planar or volumetric flaw. Ultrasonic examination with angled probes answers that on thicker sections and needs no radiation boundary. That is a real advantage in dense urban construction, on piers shared with other trades and on shipyard blocks where cordoning a work area is disruptive. Our ultrasonic testing page for San Francisco describes the technique and the report.

Whether UT may stand in for RT is a code and contract matter. ASME B31.3 and API 1104 contain provisions for ultrasonic examination of production welds, AWS D1.1 has its own ultrasonic acceptance criteria for groove welds, and ASME Section VIII allows UT in place of radiography only under specific conditions. The substitution is agreed with the owner, the engineer of record and, for code work, the authorized inspector before work is planned. In the city's special inspection process, the engineer's testing requirements and the special inspector's role must also be respected. If the answer is no, a licensed radiography contractor has to do the work, and Atlantis does not recommend or name one.

Where UT is accepted, the procedure is written to the named code and carried out by technicians qualified under the company's written practice following ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The company has no office in San Francisco, so technicians are mobilized to the site.

Level III review of radiographs, without a radiation licence

Interpreting an image needs no source and no licence. An ASNT NDT Level III can review film or digital radiographs and their technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code. Typical requests include a second opinion on a disputed indication, a check of image quality indicators, density and coverage, and review of a radiography contractor's procedure and written practice before work begins on a building frame or a pressure system.

Anoop Rayavarapu, the founder, is ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT, and this review is the use of that qualification on radiographic work. The review concerns what you supply. It does not replace the contractor's own qualified interpretation and does not make Atlantis the radiographer of record.

Owners of older San Francisco buildings and structures sometimes hold radiographs made decades ago, taken during an earlier retrofit or alteration. A Level III reading can say whether those images meet the original technique and whether they can be relied on for records.

Radiography theory and training

For teams that need to understand the method, the radiographic testing Level 2 course covers principles, exposure technique, image quality and interpretation under an employer's written practice. Hands-on work with sources must be done under the licence of the employer or a licensed training provider; Atlantis does not hold or arrange one. The San Francisco training page explains how courses and employer practical hours fit together, and the practice tests help with exam preparation.

Surface methods and related services

Atlantis also performs magnetic particle inspection and liquid penetrant testing in San Francisco for surface-breaking flaws, and statewide scope is on the California inspection services page. To discuss a weld question and how to answer it without radiography, request a quote or ask about Level III support through the Level III consulting page.

faq.q: Is radiography on my San Francisco project something Atlantis can take on?
faq.a: No. Industrial radiography requires a radiation licence under NRC or Agreement State rules, and Atlantis does not perform it in the United States, so exposure work in San Francisco is outside what we sell.

faq.q: Is ultrasonic testing accepted instead of radiography on welds?
faq.a: Sometimes. ASME B31.3, API 1104 and AWS D1.1 have ultrasonic provisions, and Section VIII permits it under conditions. The owner, engineer and authorized inspector must approve the substitution first.

faq.q: Can a Level III review radiographs that another contractor produced?
faq.a: Yes. An ASNT Level III can review film or digital images and technique sheets against ASME Section V Article 2 and the construction code, including a second read of disputed indications, with no radiation licence needed.

faq.q: Will Atlantis point me to a radiography contractor in San Francisco?
faq.a: No. We do not recommend or name radiography contractors. Choose one licensed by the state radiation control program who meets your contract and written practice requirements.

faq.q: Where can my staff learn radiography theory?
faq.a: The radiographic testing Level 2 course teaches principles, technique and interpretation. Practical work with radiation sources must be carried out under a licence held by the employer or a licensed provider.
